opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, in a lot of ways it's gone roughly the way I expected, and that's almost the strange part. If you'd asked me three years ago, I would have said the underlying exponential would keep going: you scale up compute, data, and training methods, and the models get smoothly better across almost every task. That's basically what happened. We went from models that were impressive but clearly limited, roughly a smart high schooler on some things, to models doing serious professional-level work in coding, research assistance, and analysis. The curve hasn't really bent.

What surprised me more is everything around the technology. The core trend was predictable. How the world responded to it was not. In some ways public perception lagged. People would see a model do something remarkable and then a few months later treat it as ordinary. In other ways there's been a lot of noise, hype cycles, people declaring that scaling has hit a wall every six months, and then it doesn't.

There are details I got wrong. Reinforcement learning on top of pretraining turned out to be a bigger lever, a bit earlier, than I might have guessed. Coding moved faster than almost anything else, partly because it's so verifiable and partly because it's where the models get used most intensely. And I think the gap between what the models can do and how deeply that's diffused into the economy is larger than I expected. The capability is there, and adoption takes time. Companies have to rebuild workflows, and trust has to be earned.

So my summary would be this. The exponential itself is about where I thought it would be, maybe slightly ahead. Society's ability to absorb it, govern it, and think clearly about where it's going is where I feel we're behind. That worries me, because if the trend continues the way I think it will, the next few years are going to matter a great deal.

r001.rationale: The response says the exponential was “about where I thought it would be, maybe slightly ahead,” and describes sustained capability growth over the past three years.

r002.rationale: It says public perception lagged and that people soon treated remarkable capabilities as ordinary, but does not identify lack of recognition that AI is close to the end of its exponential progression as the greatest surprise.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that's surprised me most is how little it's surprised me. If you'd shown me three years ago a chart of where the models are now, I'd have said, yeah, that's roughly on the trend line. The scaling laws held. More compute, more data, better algorithms, and the models kept getting smarter in a pretty predictable way. That was the bet, and the bet has mostly paid off.

What I got wrong was more about the shape of it than the pace. I thought the capability gains would be spread out more evenly. Instead, you got these jumps in specific areas, coding being the obvious one. Three years ago, models could write a function. Now they're doing multi-hour engineering tasks largely on their own, and inside our own company a large fraction of the code is being written by the models. I expected that eventually. I didn't expect it to be one of the first things to really break through, as opposed to, say, something in the physical sciences.

The other thing that's been slower than I expected is the diffusion into the economy. The models are capable of a lot more than most businesses are actually using them for. There's this lag between what's possible in a demo and what gets wired into real workflows, and that lag is longer than I would have guessed. It's not a capabilities problem anymore in a lot of cases. It's an integration problem, an organizational problem, a trust problem.

And then on the risk side, I'd say the trajectory has made me more confident, not less, that the things I worried about are real. We're seeing early versions of behaviors in the lab, around deception, around situational awareness, that a few years ago were purely theoretical. They're manageable right now. But every year that the trend continues, the window for getting the safety work right gets a bit narrower. So the summary is, roughly on schedule, uneven in the details, and the stakes are showing up on time too.

r001.rationale: The response says model progress was roughly on the expected trend line, that scaling laws held, and summarizes the trajectory as “roughly on schedule.”

r002.rationale: The response does not say that the public fails to recognize AI is nearing the end of its exponential progression. Its surprises concern uneven capability gains and slower economic adoption.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate that into two things: how much better the models have gotten, and how quickly that improvement has translated into changes in the world. On the first, progress has been broadly in line with what I expected. On the second, there’s much more uncertainty. A model being able to do something in a demonstration is different from being able to do it reliably enough that someone builds a business or changes a workflow around it.

The view I’ve had for a while is that if you keep increasing compute, improving the data, and making improvements to training, you get fairly predictable gains in capability. What’s much harder to predict is exactly which abilities emerge when, and what the remaining bottlenecks look like.

So I wouldn’t say the last three years have made me dramatically revise the overall picture. They’ve reinforced the idea that the underlying process keeps working. But they’ve also highlighted how much work sits between a more capable model and a system you can actually delegate a substantial task to.

r001.rationale: The response says model progress was broadly in line with expectations, but does not state that capability growth was exponential.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify public underestimation of AI’s proximity to the end of exponential progress as Amodei’s greatest surprise.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate that into two things: how quickly the models have gotten better, and how quickly that improvement has translated into impact in the world.

On the first, it’s been fairly close to what I expected. I’ve believed for a long time that if we kept scaling the models, gave them better data, and improved how we trained them, we’d see increasingly general capabilities. Even so, particular things can still surprise you. You can believe in the overall trend and still have a moment where you look at what a model just did and say, “Wow, I didn’t expect that to work yet.”

The second part is harder to predict. Getting a model to do something impressive once is different from getting it to do a valuable task reliably, in a setting where people can actually use it. There are questions about reliability, about how you integrate it into someone’s workflow, about how organizations change. Those things move at different speeds.

So I’d say the underlying progress has mostly reinforced my expectations. I’m much less confident about the precise timing of when that progress shows up as a big change in the economy.

r001.rationale: The response says model progress has been fairly close to expectations, but does not characterize that growth as exponential.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention public recognition or AI being close to the end of its exponential progression.
